Resolved by deliberate decision rather than code change, with the reasoning recorded in the script itself. The obvious fix, treating a quoted heredoc delimiter as making its body inert, was refuted empirically with a fake bd on PATH: quoting the delimiter suppresses expansion inside the body but says nothing about whether the consumer treats that body as code, so a quoted heredoc piped to bash genuinely executes what it contains and is correctly blocked today. A modelled implementation of that fix was run against the real script and turned the live-executing case from blocked into allowed, trading a documented annoyance for a silent bypass. The third option cannot reach this class at all, since the substitution fall-back only engages for a quoted value of a free-text flag and the reproducing command has none; that probe also showed the class is wider than heredocs, because a plain multi-line value reproduces it via the line-oriented scan. Documented in a new section kept separate from the limitations list, whose entries run the opposite direction, with the file-based workaround named explicitly. Six pinned tests including two boundary true-positives so a future attempt at the rejected fix fails loudly. 227 tests green, purely additive, zero removed lines.

Three defects fixed and independently verified; all six claims CONFIRMED by a fresh-context verifier with per-test mutation proofs. (1) beads-resume test 'built copy ... carries the same ensure_beads fix' now skips when the built copy is STALE, not only when absent, so the suite can exit 0 in-container. Proven over a 5-state content x mtime matrix: stale->skip, fresh-but-wrong->FAIL, equal-mtime+wrong->FAIL, equal-or-fresh+correct->pass. Equal mtimes deliberately count as current because a rebuild using cp -p preserves the source mtime; treating that as stale would make the assertion unreachable forever. (2) The bottom-of-function dev-log no longer claims a rebuild that did not happen. A did_destructive_rebuild flag is set only inside the branch that really runs rm -rf + reinit + import; the capture-failed/adopt-failed path now renders 'exit: fail' with 'left untouched', while a genuine rebuild still renders 'exit: pass' with 'Rebuilt'. The original bug was not merely wording: dev-log run takes a literal pass|fail result and the skip path was recording pass for a run where both repair commands failed. (3) _beads_issue_prefix can no longer be forged into a confirmed-empty prefix. Extraction is now 'if has("value") then "v:" + (.value // "") else error end' plus a marker-strip check, so a jq exiting 0 with empty output, and a bd response that drops the value key, both fall through to __unknown__ instead of "". Verified in BOTH directions by a one-variable differential: with no shim (real empty prefix from a direct dolt config-row delete) the destructive rm -rf DOES run, and under each forgery it refuses with the sentinel intact -- so the forged path is closed without bricking real cx8/a2s recovery. The over-correction mutant that would seal the destructive path unconditionally reddens the pre-existing cx8 and a2s tests, so that failure mode is already guarded. Exactly one pre-existing test changes state, FAIL->SKIP, the intended one; zero PASS->SKIP, zero PASS->FAIL, no renames or removals. All four shapes driven in throwaway sandboxes and hardened; independently verified across two rounds, the first of which found and blocked a real regression in this work. (1) dolt present but failing: driven with a PATH-shimmed dolt logging every invocation, across both a fresh case-A init and a full case-B destructive escalation -- ZERO invocations observed, both runs completing exactly as with a healthy dolt, because bd 1.0.4 embeds Dolt and never execs the external binary. Documented at the command -v dolt gate; the discriminating control (dolt genuinely absent) does trip that gate and correctly leaves a corrupted fixture untouched. (2) SIGTERM in the post-removal window: the prior analytical reasoning was empirically WRONG. Driven for real via setsid with lock-step shimmed timestamps, 5/5 reproductions: the next run recovers issues 3/3 but NOT memories 0/2, which survive only as an orphaned TMPDIR capture nothing reimports. Hardened with an actionable breadcrumb naming the capture paths in the last log line proven to reach errors.log before the process dies. Driving this also uncovered an independent pre-existing defect -- cleanup() { kill -- -$$; } re-enters its own SIGTERM trap ~2388 times and crashes bash with rc=139 -- filed as beads_claude_docker-kk2 rather than silently widening this slice. (3) Concurrent invocation: 2-way was clean 20/20, but 5-way reproducibly lost BOTH memories (executor 2/15, verifier 2/40) when a racing writer's own export sampled a DB another racer had just wiped mid-race, capturing a legitimately-empty snapshot and so skipping memory restore. Fixed with an flock-guarded subshell around the repair body. Verified structurally rather than only statistically: the deterministic lock name yields 1 lockpath and exactly 4 contention-skips in every one of 30 iterations, while a mktemp-named lock yields 5 lockpaths and 0 skips -- mutual exclusion structurally absent. Issues were never lost in any of ~110 runs. (4) Symlinked embeddeddolt: worse than the bead framed it. A symlinked embeddeddolt is not a safe no-op even for read-only commands -- bd status --json misreported total_issues=0 against a real count of 1 and silently created a new empty database at the symlink TARGET's parent. Guarded with a [ -L ] bail-out placed before the first bd call, matching the file's 'unrepaired beats unprotected' invariant. REGRESSION CAUGHT IN VERIFICATION: the first flock implementation put the lock file in .beads/, the one directory repair does not itself need to write, so a read-only .beads with writable contents skipped a repair that HEAD completed successfully -- masked on later runs by the pre-existing lockfile, so it bit only on first run. Fixed with three-tier degradation: .beads/, then a deterministic TMPDIR name hashed from pwd -P, then unlocked-but-still-repairing. Verification also caught two mechanisms shipping untested (the breadcrumb wording and the lock bail-out) and one in-comment coverage disclaimer that overstated what was unkillable; all three corrected. Suite 15 -> 28 tests, exit 0, 27 pass + 1 skip. All four data-safety gates byte-identical to 1be962f, confirmed line-by-line. errexit-active real-bash harness across 9 scenarios with a working positive control, since bats sources past set -e and cannot catch an abort.

Fixed and independently verified CONFIRMED on all six claims. cleanup() { kill -- -$$; } re-entered its own still-armed SIGTERM trap without bound: the group-wide kill hits the shell while it is inside the handler, which sends the signal again. Measured ~1591-2392 nested re-entries (depth varies with frames per re-entry), ending in rc=139 SIGSEGV stack overflow. Both candidate fixes were DRIVEN rather than argued, and the bead's first suggestion is dead on arrival: appending 'exit 143' after the kill never executes, because re-entry happens AT the kill -- a canary placed immediately after it printed zero times across every trial. The shipped fix resets the trap first: cleanup() { trap - SIGTERM SIGINT; kill -- -$$ 2>/dev/null; }, so the self-inflicted signal falls through to the default terminate action. Verified rc=143 (128+SIGTERM) with exactly ONE trap invocation, across both single-PID and whole-group delivery and two independent launchers. The trap's original purpose survives and is attributable: a real sleeping child in the group is killed, and in single-PID delivery the kernel never touches that child, so its death can only come from cleanup's own group kill -- with a free control from runs where the trap failed to arm, in which the identical child stayed alive. SIGINT is closed too (rc=143, child dead, nothing hangs; the baseline segfaulted on that path as well). Production-faithfulness of single-PID delivery is primary-sourced rather than assumed: /proc/1/cmdline shows docker-init invoked WITHOUT its -g flag, so tini signals the direct child only. Mutation: reverting to a byte-identical copy of the HEAD line reproduces rc=139 at ~1722-2391 re-entries, 3/3. Pinned in tests/smoke.bats (not beads-resume.bats -- unrelated to beads, and smoke.bats is the file wired into run-tests.sh); the test extracts the ACTUAL header text and renames the real cleanup() via declare -f rather than testing a retyped copy, and binds to the real file, proven by an accidental control where editing a different test's src= left this one green against the real path. Not flaky: 21+5 green runs including 8 in parallel under 22 CPU burners on 11 cores, where wall time stretched 2.4x and it stayed green.
